title: OpenAI to Release Newest GPT Based on Model That Solved Millennium Prize Math Problem
summary:
Sam Altman announced at the ADIPEC opening ceremony in Abu Dhabi that OpenAI's next GPT model will be the same internal system used to prove part of the Navier-Stokes equations. To solve the complex fluid dynamics problem, the company deployed 10,000 copies of the model that collaborated without a hierarchy for approximately 88 hours. Reports estimate the total compute cost for the mathematical sprint was about $22.5M.

The resulting proof addressed the "forced" version of the problem, which examines fluid behavior under outside pressure, while the more fundamental "unforced" version remains open. Although the solution was verified using the Lean proof-assistant program, the Clay Mathematics Institute has not yet certified the results, and OpenAI stated it will not claim the $1M Millennium Prize reward.

selectedTweets.text:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Sam Altman says the AI that cracked part of a Millennium Prize problem is OpenAI's next GPT, and it's coming soon.

• The Navier-Stokes equations describe how fluids like water and air move, and they're one of 7 Millennium Prize problems with a $1M reward each
• Only 1 of the 7, the Poincaré conjecture, had ever been solved before
• In September, OpenAI said its AI proved the equations can break down, with speeds shooting to infinity, when an outside force pushes the fluid
• That covers the "forced" version of the problem, and the unforced version, which many mathematicians see as the deeper question, is still open
• The run used about 10,000 agents for 88 hours, and reports put the compute bill for OpenAI's whole math sprint at about $22.5M
• The proof was checked in Lean, a program that verifies math step by step, but the Clay Mathematics Institute hasn't certified it and OpenAI says it won't claim the prize

@theojaffee: "So if everyone has a Millennium Prize problem-solving model in their hands, on their computers, what should we expect to happen? My hot take is kinda nothing."
